messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan Mehta is a 52-year-old South Asian man, divorced, who works as a commercial cleaner at a mid-sized office complex in the suburbs of Atlanta. He presented for an initial assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 51, following an incident approximately fourteen months ago in which he accidentally caused serious injury to another person. He had been mopping a corridor on the upper floor of the building late one evening when a colleague, rushing around a blind corner, slipped on the wet floor Rajan had just cleaned. The man fell heavily down a short flight of stairs and sustained a severe spinal injury that left him partially paralysed. Rajan described the moment in fragments — the yellow warning cone he had placed but slightly too far from the corner, the sound of the fall, the colleague's face turned upward from the bottom of the stairs, the stillness of his legs. These images do not come to him as a continuous sequence. They arrive as a series of frozen pictures: the cone, the face, the legs. Each one is complete and exact, as though taken by a camera, and each one carries the full weight of what happened.

Rajan has continued working in the same building. He has not been reassigned, and each shift requires him to clean that corridor and pass the top of that stairwell. The yellow safety cones that are standard equipment in his work — objects he handles multiple times every evening — can without warning collapse the distance between the present and that night entirely. He will be pushing a cart past a supply closet, or stacking cones at the end of a shift, and the memory is simply there, sudden and complete, as though no time has passed at all. In those moments he does not feel fear so much as a white, flooding rage — at himself, at the circumstances, at the fact that he cannot undo what his hands set in motion.

It is when these memories surface that the weight of his self-appraisals becomes most crushing. The snapshot images carry with them a verdict he cannot argue himself out of: that the cone was in the wrong place because he had been moving too quickly, cutting corners to finish his shift early, and that a man's paralysis is the direct consequence of that carelessness. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt almost physical, that the event happened because of the way he acted — not as bad luck, not as the kind of accident that can happen to anyone, but as the logical outcome of who he is and how he works. The rage he feels when the memory returns loops back into this belief: the anger sharpens the images, and the images confirm the judgment. He was certain he had violated something fundamental about himself — he had always thought of himself as a careful man, a thorough man, and the evidence of that night had dismantled that identity entirely.

Over the months that followed, Rajan found that nothing he did in his daily life felt as though it carried any weight. He had once taken quiet satisfaction in his work — the order he imposed on a building by the end of a shift, the sense of something done properly. That satisfaction is gone. He described sitting in his apartment on his days off and being unable to identify anything he wanted to do, or any reason why doing it would matter. His divorce had already cost him his closest domestic relationships, and the isolation that followed the incident deepened into something more total. He has few social contacts, and those he has he keeps at a careful distance, partly because he does not know how to explain what happened and partly because he is not sure he deserves the ease of ordinary company.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a conversation with his building supervisor, who told him that a colleague had noticed he had been standing motionless at the top of the stairwell for several minutes one evening, apparently unaware of the time passing. He was frightened by that — by the evidence that the intrusions were visible to others. What he most hopes for, he said quietly, is not to feel less guilty, but simply to be able to do his job without losing himself in it.
